item.title: We Built An Agent That Broke All of Our Security Rules. Here's What We Learned. (2026)
item.description:
We tell customers three things about securing AI agents: they need their own identities, access that fits the job they’re given, and traceability that’s separate from any human’s. That was true for us at Token as well. Then, we built an agent that broke all three by default.

This helped us think through how such agents should be defended. When a browser agent acts inside a user’s authenticated session, the application may see the user but not the agent, the delegation, or the task’s intended scope. By creating an agent that breaks all the security rules, Token learned how companies should be using identity to gain control, especially as agent use scales. Standards are coming, but there are steps security teams can take today.

The agent we would have flagged

The agent we created is named Rehearsal. Its job is to answer questions inside the Token platform by doing rather than telling. It autonomously opens pages in the browser tab, sets filters, and fills in forms.

From a security perspective, it’s a typical UI agent that runs in the user’s browser. That’s what makes it useful. But it also means the agent runs within the user’s session and has their reach.

Moreover, to the server behind the page, the agent’s clicks are inherently indistinguishable from the user’s, because nothing in a session cookie points to who the session driver is.

What controlling both sides made possible

Because Token owns both the agent and the app it runs, we can close each gap from the inside. For example, Token knows who’s driving the session because Rehearsal tells it who is.

We learned that there are multiple best practices that you can apply when you control the AI agent itself:

  • While the agent moves, dim and lock the application and clearly indicate who has control.
  • Record every move for each session, including those that were blocked.
  • Reduce the agent’s reach below the user’s. For Rehearsal, we ensure the dashboards are read-only. It can’t save anything without the user’s approval, doesn’t fill in secret fields, and never sends a call that the platform has refused. It also understands the dashboard controls through the page’s accessibility labels.

This works for our own agent, but only because it relies on access that no outside agent has.

Who has to fix it for everyone else?

We could give Rehearsal an actor, a scope, and a page map because we're the ones who wrote it. A browser agent driving your CRM or your cloud console has none of that. The app can't tell that it’s there, and the agent can't tell which field holds a secret or which button deletes a record. The session itself carries the user's identity.

The way out is to give agents their own lanes, separate from human users'. The web has started building them, but it isn't necessarily focused on holistic approaches.

The browser can mark when its agent is driving and restrict itself accordingly. Chrome auto-browse, for example, already requires a person’s approval before high-stakes actions such as payments or mass emails, limits its agent to the sites the task requires, and tags the pages the agent visits in the user’s history. Microsoft lets admins turn agentic browsing on per site and pause it before passwords and card numbers are entered.

The app can publish its actions as tools. WebMCP, a draft that Google and Microsoft are writing in a W3C community group, lets a site expose actions that an agent can call directly and flag each one as read-only or consequential. That way, the agent doesn't need to guess what a button does.

The agent can sign its requests. Web Bot Auth, now an IETF working group draft, lets a site verify which agent sent a request.

What’s missing is a layer that connects them. Each lane knows something the others don’t, and none of them passes it on. The browser knows its agent is driving, but neither Chrome nor Edge describes how to tell the app on the other end. A WebMCP tool runs inside the user’s session, with the user’s rights, so it doesn’t, by itself, narrow what the agent can reach. Web Bot Auth names the agent, but the draft makes it plain that it doesn’t cover delegation, so it omits the person the agent works for.

The app ends up holding on to pieces of context rather than delivering something actionable.

Now consider that the agents are arriving faster than the standards. Agent-friendly isn’t enough on its own. Every lane built for agents should carry the agent’s identity, a verifiable link to the person it acts for, and a scope narrower than that person’s. Together, those three signals give an application the minimum context it needs to make an authorization decision. Otherwise, a faster lane is just a faster path to the misuse of privilege.

What security teams can do before standards catch up

Waiting for standardization is not an option. You need to start discovering agentic browsers and extensions as soon as possible, including the users whose sessions they borrow. And while you can’t tell who clicked, you can choose which clicks need a person by adding a step-up check such as a passkey prompt. 

  • Inventory browser agents, agentic extensions, and endpoint agents that can act through authenticated sessions and map them to users and owners.
  • Trace every AI agent consumer, so you know which people (and other agents) are using each individual agent
  • Review every identity that each individual agent has access to
  • Identify potential attack paths that use agents to bypass access controls
  • Require explicit approval or step-up authentication before sensitive or irreversible application actions.
  • Ask critical SaaS vendors whether their audit records distinguish agent activity from human activity and whether they support task-scoped delegation.

Until browsers and applications can carry agent identity, human delegation, and task scope together, companies should treat every agent using a human session as delegated access that must be discovered, constrained, and audited.

item.title: Over 35,000 Grok-Built Apps Exposed Online, Some Leaking Confidential Data and Passwords (2026)
item.description:
Of the 37,571 Grok-built apps that security company Claroc found online, 35,578 were open to anyone without a sign-in, the researchers said yesterday.

They included 24 apps built by staff at the social network X and at SpaceXSI, the company that makes the Grok AI assistant. Most of the open apps were games, landing pages, and calculators, but about 1 in 10 contained internal business or personal data.

The staff apps included a confidential onboarding plan for a new sales hire, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, and an X advertising proposal to a U.S. federal agency marked confidential. SpaceXSI, formerly known as xAI, has since taken down all 24 staff apps but not other users' apps, the researchers said.

Besides those staff apps, the open apps contained internal data from 30 other organizations the researchers could identify, across fields ranging from construction and energy to healthcare and defense. Of those, 26 have more than 1,000 employees, and 6 are Fortune 500 companies.

According to the researchers' estimate in their report, roughly 2% of the open apps contained material serious enough to rate as high or critical.

The exposed material included a hospital group's searchable list of more than 3,500 employees, an intensive care briefing on a single patient, a fire department's live shift board, and a contractor's timesheet whose code held every employee's password in plain text.

Grok can build a working app from a description typed into its chat, a feature its maker opened to every Grok plan on August 19. This chat builder shares the Grok Build name with a separate terminal coding tool, whose repository uploads were reported on July 14.

Each published app gets its own subdomain of grok.me, and its creator chooses who can open it, according to the company's launch announcement.

No app goes public until its creator clicks Publish. In the paid account the researchers used, the next step offered 3 access settings: "Anyone with the link", "Invited users" and "Only you". "Anyone with the link" was already selected.

The setting matters because an app's address does not stay secret, the researchers say. Opening an app makes the visitor's computer look up its subdomain in DNS. Passive DNS services record such lookups, and anyone with an account can search those records by pattern.

Grok suggests 4 random words as each app's name, and about half of the names the researchers found followed that pattern. Such names are hard to guess, but that does not protect an app whose name already sits in a searchable list.

ChatGPT's app builder also puts each app on its own subdomain. But when the researchers shared an app there, its access was set to "Only me" until they changed it. A ChatGPT app address found in DNS data would lead to an app that only its owner can open, they say.

The researchers found the Grok app names using common subdomain discovery methods and loaded each app's first page once, without signing in.

To see what protection Grok adds on its own, the researchers built 2 test apps with made-up data and published both with the access setting already selected, "Anyone with the link".

The first, a contact list, got a database but no sign-in. Without signing in, the researchers added a row from a private browser window, and the next visitor saw it.

The second, a customer list for a 4-person sales team, got sign-in buttons that Grok added on its own: "Continue with Google" and "Continue with X". But the code Grok wrote added each person who signed in to the team before checking whether they belonged, so the check always passed.

An uninvited Google account belonging to someone other than the owner got in, viewed every customer, edited one record, and deleted another.

The researchers ran these tests only on their own apps. They did not test whether any of the open apps they found would accept such changes.

The researchers reported their findings to SpaceXSI on Sunday through the address in its security.txt file, including 2 of the staff apps. They reported the other 22 on Monday.

By the time the researchers published yesterday, the company had not replied to their report, but it had answered a reporter's questions about the research.

As the researchers describe, the company said Grok apps stay private until their creator shares them. Publishing takes several steps, including choosing between "Only you" and "Anyone with the link," as well as a legal disclaimer. Employee accounts are set to "Only you" by default.

Even so, 24 apps built by staff at the company and at X were open to anyone, the researchers say.

With their report, the researchers had asked the company to make "Only you" the default and to add an option that limits an app to a company's own email domain.

The company's response did not state that it would contact the owners of other open apps, according to the researchers. They have started emailing the affected organizations themselves and had emailed 3 by the time they published. They withheld every app address and title from the report.

On October 18, the same researchers published Muse research showing that pages shared from Meta's Muse AI agent could be found through passive DNS. Meta disabled sharing, then announced a sharing fix on October 22 that gave shared items new addresses.

How to Check Your Organization's Grok Apps

Claroc, which sells tools to find and secure apps built with AI, recommends these checks:

  • Find out which AI app builders your staff uses. Builders such as Grok, Lovable, Replit, v0, Bolt, Base44 and Google AI Studio can be used without IT setting them up or a company account.
  • If you have access to passive DNS data, look up the builders' domains and open any results in a private browser window.
  • Make sure any Grok app with internal data is set to "Invited users" or "Only you", and that a stranger gets an error page.
  • Try to sign in with an account from outside your company. If it gets in, the app needs a list of who is allowed.
  • Check the scripts each app loads for names, email addresses and passwords, and unpublish apps that have no owner.

In the researchers' tests, setting an app to "Only you" caused it to return a 401 error to a stranger for both the page and its data, and unpublishing took an app offline within seconds.

item.title: Hackers Target Qlik Sense Servers With Reverse Shells, Stage ActiveMQ and Veeam Exploits (2026)
item.description:
Threat actors have been observed targeting Qlik Sense servers to unsuccessfully deliver PowerShell reverse shell commands against multiple environments in October 2026.

Cynet's CyOps and Research teams said they identified the suspicious activity in October 2026 against several E.U.-based customers within a narrow window of just over three minutes.

The activity has been found to share some level of overlap with a November 2023 campaign documented by Arctic Wolf in which threat actors linked to the CACTUS ransomware operation likely weaponized then-newly-disclosed flaws in Qlik Sense to obtain initial access to target environments.

The vulnerabilities in question, which were patched by Qlik Sense in August and September 2023, impact Qlik Sense Enterprise for Windows -

  • CVE-2023-41265 (CVSS score: 9.6) - An HTTP tunneling vulnerability that could lead to privilege escalation and allow an attacker to execute HTTP requests on the backend server hosting the repository application.
  • CVE-2023-41266 (CVSS score: 8.2) - A path traversal vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to generate an anonymous session and perform HTTP requests to unauthorized endpoints.
  • CVE-2023-48365 (CVSS score: 9.6) - An unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability that stems from improper validation of HTTP headers, allowing an attacker to elevate their privilege by tunneling HTTP requests and execute HTTP requests on the backend server.

It's worth noting that CVE-2023-48365 (aka DoubleQlik) is an incomplete fix for CVE-2023-41265.

In November 2023 CACTUS ransomware campaign, threat actors were observed exploiting the flaws to establish a foothold and download additional payloads to establish persistence and remote control by deploying ManageEngine Unified Endpoint Management and Security (UEMS), AnyDesk, and Plink.

The latest activity detected by Cynet involves the use of a PowerShell command containing a one-line reverse shell that connects to "45.115.26[.]23" on port 4455. The exact vulnerability exploited to break into Qlik Sense servers is currently not known.

"The command was executed under scheduler.exe, resembling the 2023 Cactus Qlik intrusions," the cybersecurity company said.

Although attempts to spawn the reverse shell were blocked, Cynet's testing of the reverse shell in a controlled environment has revealed that the interactive communication channel is used to conduct reconnaissance and deliver a PowerShell script for enabling persistence.

This is achieved by means of a Windows Go reverse shell that connects to "45.115.26[.]23:4456." The backdoor is then used to look for actively running processes related to Apache ActiveMQ. On Linux, the malware also attempts to collect system information and read "/etc/shadow" and "/etc/passwd" files.

A second variant of the PowerShell script attempts to install OpenSSH and creates a scheduled task named "WinUpdCheck" that launches a PowerShell reverse shell written to "C:\ProgramData\ssh\winc.ps1" at five-minute intervals. 

"If sshd remained unavailable, it downloaded OpenSSH-Win64.zip from the staging server, extracted it, and ran install-sshd.ps1," Cynet said. "It set sshd to automatic startup, started the service, and added an inbound firewall rule for TCP 22. The archive was a legitimate OpenSSH package reused by the operator."

Further analysis of the infrastructure has uncovered an exposed directory ("45.115.26[.]23:8012") consisting of a custom Go backdoor for Windows, SSH persistence scripts, an ActiveMQ exploit for CVE-2023-46604, and a modified public Veeam toolchain for CVE-2024-40711, indicating the threat actor is possibly laying the groundwork for broader attacks.

item.title: AntiFox AI Pentesting Platform Linked to Attacks That Accessed AWS Production Secrets (2026)
item.description:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a campaign in which an emerging agentic penetration testing platform called AntiFox has been used to steal Amazon Web Services (AWS) credentials and pivot laterally into compromised environments.

"In several recently observed intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were associated with confirmed malicious actions against internet-facing web services and associated AWS environments," Arctic Wolf Labs said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

The activity has been observed chaining together web exploitation and web shell deployment to facilitate configuration discovery, credential validation, cloud-service enumeration, secret access, and storage operations.

AntiFox, available for download from GitHub, has been described as an artificial intelligence (AI)-driven autonomous penetration testing platform that's built atop the "solid foundation" of ARTEX. As of writing, the project has been forked 251 times and starred 474 times.

On its README page, the project maintainer states -

Given an authorized target, a planner / worker / main-agent multi-agent system runs the full engagement over a dual-graph core (a global asset graph + a per-task exploration graph) — recon → attack-surface discovery → exploitation → finding capture → report delivery — fully observable, interactive, and deliverable

Unlike most automated pentest tools that are "great at discovery, but stop at discovery," AntiFox puts its weight on delivery — turning what the AI finds into a report that an engineer can understand, reproduce, back with evidence, and hand straight to the client.

According to Arctic Wolf, some of the initial access activity is associated with a compromised internet-facing Internet Information Services (IIS) application. The access is then leveraged to create an ASPX web shell using "w3wp.exe," the IIS worker process, and run operating system commands to perform the following actions -

  • Run PowerShell commands to locate web.config files and configuration backups
  • Read application settings and database connection strings
  • Enumerate debug and error-log directories
  • Attempts to connect to an internal production database using a credential extracted from the application configuration
  • Copy configuration and log files into a web-accessible upload directory

"On a compromised IIS server, commands run through w3wp.exe identified the execution context with whoami, enumerated the application directory, checked permissions with icacls, and tested the ability to write files into the web root," Arctic Wolf said.

"The creation of an ASPX web shell by w3wp.exe, followed by command execution through the same IIS worker process, suggests compromise through the affected web application."

The precise vulnerability used to achieve code execution on the IIS server is not known. In other attacks, the threat actor is said to have started with a valid AWS credential obtained through as-yet-undetermined means.

AntiFox Demo

Specifically, this involved abusing valid IAM identities to validate credentials and enumerate dozens of services, including IAM, EC2, S3, Lambda, Secrets Manager, KMS, RDS, ECS, EKS, Redshift, Athena, Glue, Systems Manager, API Gateway, CloudWatch, CloudFormation, DynamoDB, and Amazon Bedrock.

While a majority of these authenticated cross-service API requests ended up with an "AccessDenied" error, some of the discovery and secret-access operations were successful, according to the cybersecurity company.

item.title: Critical Zoom Workplace Flaw Could Allow Unauthenticated Remote Privilege Escalation (2026)
item.description:
Zoom has released software updates to address two security flaws impacting Zoom Workplace for Windows, including a critical bug that could result in privilege escalation on affected systems.

The vulnerabilities are listed below -

  • CVE-2026-108186 (CVSS score: 9.6) - An improper input validation vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated user to conduct an escalation of privilege via network access.
  • CVE-2026-108187 (CVSS score: 8.1) - An origin validation vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated user to conduct an escalation of privilege via network access.

Successful exploitation of either of the shortcomings could permit remote attackers to escalate privileges without requiring any special permissions or access.

While CVE-2026-108187 affects Zoom Workplace for Windows before version 7.1.5, CVE-2026-108186 impacts versions starting from 7.1.0 and before 7.1.8.

Earlier this July, the popular videoconferencing platform shipped fixes for another improper input validation flaw impacting Zoom Workplace for Windows (CVE-2026-53412, CVSS score: 9.8) that could enable an unauthenticated user to take control of accounts.

Although Zoom makes no mention of the vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild, users are advised to apply the latest patches to mitigate potential threats.

item.title: ScreenConnect Attacks Target at Least 288 Endpoints Across 48 Organizations With Rogue Clients (2026)
item.description:
ConnectWise has taken the precautionary step of disabling five third-party extensions in partner environments following reports of unauthorized access.

In an advisory posted on its site, the company said there is no evidence that the incident involves a compromise of its infrastructure or a vulnerability in the ScreenConnect software.

"Our initial assessment suggests the activity may involve a threat actor's abuse of independent third-party extensions installed in partner environments," it said. "We are continuing to validate this assessment. The initial access method and full scope remain under investigation."

ConnectWise has identified about 400 partner environments with at least one of the third-party extensions installed. It also emphasized that the presence of the extensions alone does not indicate or establish compromise.

While these extensions provide an API capable of executing remote commands, access to that API is secured by a passphrase configured by the partner during setup, it added. The list of extensions identified for precautionary disabling is below -

  • Labtech Plus
  • RMM Plus
  • RMM+
  • RMM Plus Password Link
  • RMM+ Password Link

ConnectWise also said it has urged on-premises partners to disable the extensions, and is recommending all partners to ensure security controls are running, preserve suspicious activity logs, and stay vigilant for -

  • Unusual sign-ins, unfamiliar locations, repeated login failures, and unexpected multi-factor authentication (MFA) prompts
  • New administrator accounts or changes to user permissions
  • Unexpected extension installations, remote commands, and Toolbox activity
  • Unapproved remote-access software on customer devices and technician workstations
  • Unexpected support requests, password-reset messages, and software downloads through a trusted channel

The company has shared the following indicators of compromise (IoCs) -

  • IP addresses:
    • 185.99.255[.]28
    • 155.94.150[.]39
  • Domains and URLs: 
    • ns[.]mo7sen[.]dev
    • ns[.]mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php?p=4
    • sc[.]payproofkit[.]com
    • cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com
    • newnewnew[.]gotdns[.]org
    • Soxnewwork[.]homedns[.]org
  • Artifacts:
    • sckit-run.bat
    • sckit-decoder.ps1
    • TrapWatch.ps1
    • Panel-Lateral.ps1
    • Run-Lateral-Full.bat
    • runnew.cmd
    • ToolboxRelayUploader.exe
    • Sqlite3.exe

Cybersecurity company Huntress, which is also tracking the activity, said it has observed attackers using access to cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels to push Run commands with an aim to install rogue ScreenConnect clients on at least 288 managed endpoints across 48 organizations. The activity was first detected on November 11, 2026, at around 5:47 p.m. UTC.

Huntress told The Hacker News that it has not seen evidence of a new vulnerability, but noted the exact method through which the attacker got panel access remains unclear. Current telemetry points to compromised credentials or hijacked operator sessions to gain initial access, it said.

The overall attack unfolds in a worm-like fashion using a two-step process -

  • Initial access: Attackers use a compromised ScreenConnect panel's Run Command feature to deploy a rogue ScreenClient client across endpoints, creating a persistent backdoor that no longer depends on the original panel.
  • Lateral movement: When a technician connects to an infected endpoint through ScreenConnect, the malware can spread back to their workstation, steal saved browser sessions and authentication tokens, and pivot to other ScreenConnect panels the technician has access to.

"The rogue clients deliver SCKit, a custom malicious toolkit that establishes persistent remote access and creates a relay trap for intercepting session cookies," Huntress researchers Ben Nahorney and Susannah Matt said.

"The infection path works in two stages: from an infected endpoint to a technician who connects to it, and from a technician's workstation to every endpoint their panel can connect to. However, not all functionality has been observed during observed incidents; some functionality has been discovered through analysing the payloads."

SCKit is delivered as an encrypted payload and via a Base64-encoded dropper ("sckit-run.bat"), which then contacts a remote server to fetch a PowerShell payload ("sckit-decoder.ps1") that's responsible for launching the toolkit.

Other components of the malware are designed to add Microsoft Defender exclusions, install a second attacker-controlled ScreenConnect client, create a scheduled task named "TrapWatch," and replace the legitimate ScreenConnect installation with an attacker-controlled copy.

There are signs that at least one of the scripts is generated by a large language model (LLM) based on the detailed source code references and comments that explain its functionality.

"Going beyond what we've observed, we've reconstructed an additional functionality intended to spread from a technician's workstation to the ScreenConnect panel," Huntress said. "This has been discovered from analysis of its scripts, configuration, and tools. To date we have not observed a successful jump from an infected endpoint to a technician workstation, or from that workstation to other endpoints."

This involves abusing the connection to fetch a dropper ("Run-Lateral-Full.bat"), which then connects to an external server ("ns.mo7sen[.]dev") to download a loader that gathers the workstation's unique ID, sends it back to  the attacker, and returns a tailored encrypted kit for that specific workstation -

  • "Panel-Lateral.ps1," which in conjunction with "LabConfig.ps1," steals the .aspxauth session cookie from the workstation and attempts to replay the cookie against the panel and get the tokens necessary to enumerate any other sessions the technician can access.
  • "ToolboxRelayUploader.exe," which leverages access gained to any other sessions to upload a payload, "WithUninstall.ps1," to the panel's Shared Toolbox.

"A panel request tells every reachable session to run the toolbox item," Huntress said. "This payload is designed to run as SYSTEM on those endpoints, installing the trap and extending the cycle. Roughly 60 seconds after the broadcast, ToolboxRelayUploader.exe deletes the Shared Toolbox item."

To add to the concern, the threat actor has been observed tagging each compromised managed service provider (MSP) with a sequential number. Huntress said the tags it has observed start partway through the sequence, indicating other MSPs may have been compromised earlier. ScreenConnect users are advised to check their Run Command history even if they haven't received alerts.

In a separate alert, Sophos said it has also observed unauthorized ScreenConnect client deployments following the same modus operandi. The activity has originated from three ScreenConnect instance IDs -

  • d905b2b1b165d0a9
  • 4b8f4089ddaac6a9
  • df1f7ef0cfacd0d8

It's suspected that these are compromised instances that are being used to execute commands and deploy additional malicious instances, whose IDs are below -

  • 2588ef5c15954b10
  • ed630cc2c873b091

"Curl.exe downloaded ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi from 185.99.255[.]28 to C:\Windows\TEMP\sc.msi," Sophos explained. "A ScreenConnect-generated command file then launched msiexec.exe to install the client silently. The researchers also observed ScreenConnect scripts staging batch files and using PowerShell with execution-policy bypass to retrieve a second-stage script from ns[.]mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php?p=4."

(This is a developing story. Please check back for more details.)

item.title: Critical Apache HTTP/2 Flaw Could Let Unauthenticated Attackers Execute Code Remotely (2026)
item.description:
A critical flaw in Apache HTTP Server's HTTP/2 module, mod_http2, can let a remote attacker run code on the server. Tracked as CVE-2026-119618, it affects versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 and is fixed in version 2.4.71, released yesterday.

Only servers with HTTP/2 enabled are affected, according to Red Hat, which ships the server as part of Red Hat Enterprise Linux.

An attacker who can reach the server needs no authentication to exploit the flaw and could take full control of the server process, the Linux vendor says. It rates the flaw 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale.

The vendor's assessment, published yesterday, also says "public research has demonstrated a reliable exploit" against a server in its default configuration with mod_http2 enabled. item.title: Attacker Used 4,837 Hijacked GitHub Accounts to Run a CI Secret Stealer in 1,806+ Repositories (2026)
item.description:
Starting Tuesday, an attacker used stolen credentials for 4,837 GitHub accounts to plant a secret stealer in repositories those accounts could write to, according to Aikido Security, a security software company.

The stealer is built to take the secrets and cloud credentials that a repository's CI workflows can reach. It ran in at least 1,806 repositories, where the attacker has likely collected those credentials, the company says.

Each attack started with a pull request titled docs: dependency audit notes, opened from a branch named wfx-docs to test whether the account could write to the repository. These test pull requests were opened in 61,764 repositories, and the stealer followed in some of them.

In a separate analysis, researchers at SafeDep, which sells software supply chain security tools, counted 8,093 repositories that received malicious commits between 12:46 UTC on Tuesday and 04:36 UTC today. That count covers every repository that received malicious commits, not only those where the stealer ran. Their search covered only the default branches of public repositories, so the true total is higher, the researchers say.

In 7,309 of those repositories, the stealer was added to an existing workflow. In 771, it came as an npm postinstall hook, which also runs on a developer's machine during npm install.

After pushing the stealer, the attacker usually reverted the change within minutes. Where the stealer ran, its logs were deleted, usually along with the run itself. In those repositories, every secret and cloud role available to the workflows should be treated as compromised.

More pull requests with the same title were opened early today, after the company's own GitHub search ended on Wednesday, a check by The Hacker News found. Three that were checked, opened between 05:04 and 05:38 UTC, came from wfx-docs branches. It is not clear whether the stealer followed.

Any account that opened one of the attacker's test pull requests is compromised, even if the stealer never ran, Aikido said in its technical analysis. The analysis does not explain how the attacker obtained the credentials.

SafeDep's researchers advise owners of affected repositories to revoke the commit author's tokens, OAuth app grants, SSH keys, and sessions, and to turn on 2FA. Owners should also rotate every secret and variable the repository can read. Anyone who ran npm install on an affected commit should treat that machine as compromised and rotate its keys.

In most other repositories that received a test, nothing was pushed afterward, or the stealer did not run due to the repository's settings or the account's permissions. The figures cover only the public repositories the company could see.

The tests also reached repositories that the compromised accounts did not own. Of the test pull requests, 10,431 were submitted via collaborator or organization access, and 92% of those were still open when the company checked.

Signs a Repository Was Hit

Check for these signs, from Tuesday onward, in any repository you can write to:

  • Branch: wfx-docs
  • Branch: chore/[a-z0-9]{8}, short-lived
  • Branch: ci-check-[0-9]{4}
  • Pull request title: docs: dependency audit notes
  • Commit message: ci: refresh build cache, which adds about 1,500 lines to an existing workflow
  • Commit message: chore: add ci helper, which adds a .ci-xxxxxx.sh script and a postinstall hook in package.json that runs it on any npm install
  • Commit message: chore: add dependency audit workflow, which adds .github/workflows/build-audit-xxxxxx.yml on a chore/ branch
  • Commit message: chore: initial commit, pushed before a new workflow file in an empty repository
  • Commit message: ci: restore
  • Commit message: ci: cleanup
  • SHA-256 (stealer script): 89695abb392d5cfd4972672961e644bb46baa98aa1ed7173c2a2816c762735cf
  • IP: 194.150.166[.]244:8080/exfil
  • IP: 18.143.168[.]96:8080/exfil
  • IP: 153.75.82[.]159:8080

A repository can show no wfx-loot artifacts, wfx- cache entries, or WFX-BEGIN step summaries and still have lost data. A missing run number on the attacker's commit is the more reliable sign that the stealer ran.

The stealer sends data by HTTP POST to the addresses above or to a Telegram chat, the SafeDep researchers found. In a sample of 200 payload commits, about a fifth used Telegram only.

The stealer is built to collect credentials from every source on the runner, according to the company. They include GitHub Actions secrets and variables, the workflow's GITHUB_TOKEN, OIDC and Actions runtime tokens, keys for AI services, and secrets in the memory of the runner's own processes. It reads credential files for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, PyPI, SSH, and other tools from their usual locations.

It also copies the repository, its last 100 commits, and recent workflow artifacts. On self-hosted runners, it takes cloud credentials from instance metadata as well as Docker container state and systemd units.

The stealer also has settings for private repositories, and the company says that suggests it may be running in them.

The stealer is designed to use those credentials to reach deeper into cloud accounts. It exchanges GitHub OIDC tokens for AWS, GCP, and Azure sessions, and on AWS it can create long-lived access keys for IAM users.

Some of its steps are built to survive credential rotation. It can rewrite an AWS role's trust policy to open the role to any AWS account.

It can also add federated identity credentials with the prefix wfx-ci- to Azure AD applications. Workflows in the compromised repository can then sign in to Azure without a stored secret, even after all tokens are rotated.

To find these backdoors, the researchers suggest checking for:

  • Entra ID: federated credentials named wfx-ci-* that you did not create
  • AWS CloudTrail: AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity or AssumeRole sessions named wfx-*, followed by CreateAccessKey or UpdateAssumeRolePolicy
  • GCP: GenerateAccessToken and SignJwt calls from your GitHub workload identity pool
  • Vault: JWT logins from the GitHub OIDC issuer

The stealer reached at least one Packagist package and one Go module through automated publishing triggers. At least 50 of the compromised users appear to publish packages for npm, Go, Packagist, PyPI, or crates.

The attacker appears to be after CI secrets rather than trying to spread through packages, the company says.

Version 3.14.3 of the Packagist package digitalelvis/neuronai-studio is malicious, and the company advises treating any machine that installed or opened it as compromised. Its package listing shows the version was published on Wednesday. Early today, the version was still listed, under a notice that versions of the package had been flagged as malware.

A normal composer install does not run the stealer, but running npm install inside the package's vendor directory does, the researchers found. Users should block v3.14.3 and pin v3.14.2 or earlier.

Two versions of the Go module github.com/onuragtas/docker-env, v1.0.278 and v1.0.280, carry the stealer only in a GitHub Actions workflow file. The Go code and release binaries are unchanged, and Go builds never run workflow files, so users of the module may not have been affected. The company still recommends removing those versions.

The researchers also found the stealer in another Go module, github.com/vkuznet/gocurl, in pseudo-version v0.0.0-20261111095532-8d5aad0cb0da, inside a workflow that has never run. Users should block that pseudo-version.

The stealer also reached 28 WebdriverIO repositories through commits authored as the bot account wdio-bot. No package release was affected, but the bot's token should be treated as stolen.

The company found that the accounts used this week overlap with those hit in GhostAction's October wave, in which stolen GitHub accounts pushed secret-stealing workflows into repositories.

Accounts hit in October were about 1,000 times more likely than other active accounts to be used this week. In more than 100 repositories, the new stealer was added to October's workflow files, leaving the older step that sends data out in place.

Aikido said, "we don't attribute November to the same actor at this stage," because the infrastructure, tools, and methods differ, and stolen credentials often end up with several attackers.

Correction (November 12, 2026): An earlier version of this article said the stealer sent data only by HTTP POST to two addresses and that the attacker reverted each change within a minute. A second analysis found a third server, a Telegram channel, and changes left in place for longer.

item.title: Node.js Fixes 16 Flaws, Including HTTP/2 Bugs That Crash Servers and Leak Other Connections' Data (2026)
item.description:
A flaw fixed in Node.js this week lets unauthenticated clients crash servers that use the runtime's built-in HTTP/2 support on the 24.x and 26.x release lines. A second HTTP/2 flaw can cause a server to send a client pieces of its memory, including responses intended for other connections.

Fixed versions were released for all three supported lines: 22.23.5, 24.22.3, and 26.13.1.

The crash flaw, CVE-2026-123863, needs only a default HTTP/2 server that replies before the request body has fully arrived. The Node.js project calls that behavior typical. The crash works over both TLS and cleartext connections.

The memory flaw, CVE-2026-123866, affects all three lines. From 24.22.0 and 26.9.0 onward, a client alone can trigger it. On 22.x and older 24.x and 26.x builds, it can still be triggered when the server itself closes a stream partway through a response, for example after an idle timeout.

A separate flaw in Node.js HTTPS servers, CVE-2026-123864, can allow an unauthenticated client to read memory from other connections, "including TLS private keys and other users' requests," the project says. It affects all three supported lines.

The flaw needs a handler that calls res.flushHeaders() before the request body has fully arrived and later calls res.end() with data. Reading the leaked memory also needs a route that sends back or stores a request body. Plain HTTP servers built with node:http are not affected.

The release fixes 16 vulnerabilities in Node.js itself, seven of them rated high. The other four high-rated flaws, and the servers they affect, are:

  • CVE-2026-123865: a client can make any default HTTP/2 server hold memory and file descriptors permanently, on all three lines.
  • CVE-2026-123874: a client can corrupt server memory on 24.x and 26.x when the server serves files with stream.respondWithFile() or stream.respondWithFD(). On all three lines, canceling such downloads can also crash the server (CVE-2026-123875, rated medium).
  • CVE-2026-126051: a client can crash a TLS server on 24.x and 26.x if the server uses the SNICallback, OCSPRequest, newSession or resumeSession hooks, or server.addContext().
  • CVE-2026-123872: on a TLS server with stricter client-certificate rules for some hostnames, a client approved for another hostname can switch to a stricter one during TLS 1.2 renegotiation without meeting its rules. All three lines are affected.

The eight flaws above are all in Node.js's own HTTP/2, HTTPS and TLS server code, so they matter where a Node.js process accepts those connections itself.

Updating to the fixed version for each line is the only fix in the project's security advisory. It lists no workaround for servers that cannot update yet.

End-of-life lines, including 20.x and 25.x, get no fix in this release, and the project says such versions are always affected.

The advisory does not report any attacks using the flaws. It also does not say whether servers that met the conditions for the HTTPS flaw should replace their TLS keys or other secrets after updating.

Five of the flaws, including CVE-2026-123863 and CVE-2026-123864, were reported by Chris Rohlf in collaboration with Claude and Anthropic Research, according to the advisory.

item.title: Critical Pre-Auth MongoDB Flaw (CVE-2026-118383) Can Crash Lagging Servers on Failover
item.description:
A critical flaw in MongoDB Server allows an unauthenticated attacker to send two requests that trigger a crash on the database server. The crash occurs only if that server is later chosen to take over as the main server while it still lacks some recent changes.

MongoDB, the company that makes the database, released fixed versions earlier this week.

The affected servers are members of a replica set, a group of MongoDB servers that keep copies of the same data. One member, the primary, serves as the main server and handles all new writes, while the others replicate them. If the primary becomes unavailable, the other members hold an election to pick a new primary.

Researchers at Datadog Security Labs reproduced the crash in a lab and published their findings yesterday. On vulnerable versions, turning on authentication does not stop the two requests. An attacker cannot make the targeted member fall behind or win an election, or see when either happens, the researchers said.

item.title: PTC Patches Critical Windchill and FlexPLM Flaw That Could Enable Remote Code Execution (2026)
item.description:
PTC has released patches for a new critical vulnerability impacting Windchill and FlexPLM software that, if successfully exploited, could result in remote code execution.

The security flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-126325, carries a CVSS v4 score of 9.2 out of a maximum of 10.0.

It has been described as a case of improper input validation and deserialization of untrusted data that could result in remote code execution via crafted requests.

"A critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability has been reported in PTC Windchill and PTC FlexPLM," according to a description of the flaw on CVE.org. "The vulnerability may be exploited through the deserialization of untrusted data."

The CVE record lists the following versions as affected -

  • PTC Windchill: 11.0 M030, 11.1 M020, 11.2.1.0, 12.0.2.0, 12.1.2.0, 13.0.2.0, 13.1.0.0, 13.1.1.0, 13.1.2.0, 13.1.3.0, 13.1.4.0
  • PTC FlexPLM: 11.0 M030, 11.1 M020, 11.2.1.0, 12.0.2.0, 12.1.2.0, 13.0.2.0, 13.1.0.0, 13.1.1.0, 13.1.2.0, 13.1.3.0

"If your Windchill or FlexPLM environment is hosted by PTC, the patches have been applied on their behalf. No action is required on your part," PTC said in a statement posted on its website.

"If your Windchill or FlexPLM environment is not hosted by PTC, we urge you to apply the patch as soon as possible to help protect your systems."

The disclosure comes nearly five months after another critical remote code execution (RCE) issue in Windchill and FlexPLM (CVE-2026-12569, CVSS score: 9.3) came under active exploitation.

Then, in July 2026, it emerged that threat actors linked to the Cl0p ransomware operation were weaponizing the flaw as part of a data extortion campaign designed to drop JSP web shells and exfiltrate sensitive product data from manufacturing companies and industrial enterprises.

"PTC software is a textbook target for initial access brokers and ransomware operators and a significant enabler of triple extortion campaigns," Yordan Ganchev, principal threat intelligence specialist at watchTowr, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.

"It allows malicious actors to reach far and wide within victim networks, encrypt and exfiltrate proprietary data, and disrupt industrial processes. In many cases, the impact across these environments has downstream implications for time-sensitive manufacturing, logistics, and fulfillment processes, resulting in material costs per hour of downtime."

Organizations running PTC Windchill and FlexPLM products are recommended to patch exposed systems as soon as possible and monitor for signs of code execution, backdoor access, or web shells on the host. If patching is not an immediate option, it's essential to apply network restrictions to limit the risk of compromise.

item.title: Calendar Invites and Live Proxies: Inside a Google Session Hijacking Campaign (2026)
item.description:
Since mid-August 2026, a phishing operation has been stealing live Google sessions from corporate users. Every check defenders normally lean on to judge a link came back clean, and the operator designed it that way on purpose.

The Threat Research team at Material Security spotted the campaign and has since taken down hundreds of attacker domains in an effort the team calls Operation CloudFire. Here’s what the researchers found.

The lure: Google Calendar invites

The messages show up as Google Calendar invites. Some arrive by BCC, and many come from an organization the recipient has already traded email with. The pretexts are deliberately boring: voicemail notifications, RFP and RFI requests, court summonses, and missed payment notices. Nothing about them stands out in a busy inbox.

Most of the links point to Google itself. The usual pattern runs through Google’s own /url redirector, with the real destination tucked into a query parameter. Other waves used share.google and Drive file links the same way, and one variant leaned on Intuit transaction notification links. Whenever a message gets scored, the domain, certificate, and reputation on display are all legitimate.

The capture: a reverse proxy in front of Google sign-in

Once a victim clicks through, the attacker runs a live reverse proxy in front of the real Google sign-in page. The victim types a password, gets a genuine prompt, and approves it while the operator watches in real time. The server passes each second factor along to Google as it comes in, whether that’s an SMS code, an authenticator code, Google’s Tap-Yes number matching, or phone-based account recovery. None of those controls stop the session from being captured.

The framework behind it, known as Nyasher, has been publicly documented since February, after researchers found a hardcoded key in its JavaScript.

Why the usual controls stay quiet

Reputation systems answer questions about ownership. They ask who registered a domain, what else it has hosted, and whether anyone has complained about it. This campaign was built so every one of those answers came back harmless.

It works in three layers. The first is Google’s redirector, which gives the initial hop a trusted Google URL. The second is a Cloudflare Turnstile challenge, and in some builds it’s the real widget served from Cloudflare’s own infrastructure. The third is the password capture page, and that’s where things get tricky for defenders. There’s no static site to scan. JavaScript builds the page in the browser after the visitor clears the challenge, so a crawler has nothing to fetch and a proxy log has nothing to record. As far as the researchers know, nobody had scanned those pages before the campaign was documented.

The infrastructure is also meant to be thrown away. Early waves used many lure domains spread across several registrars, and most were registered just days before use. Receiving endpoints went live one to twenty days ahead of the wave they served. One wildcard certificate was issued 46 minutes before the domain it covers was even registered. Blocking any single piece costs the operator a few dollars and an afternoon.

What stopping it took

Researchers tracked the campaign from the start, following each variant as lures, gates, and endpoints rotated. Once detections were in place, they caught more than 99% of the malicious messages, with a reclassification rate of 0.01%. It’s been steady work, since the attacker kept changing tactics, themes, and lure text to slip past static, machine learning, and agentic detections.

What worked was refusing to let any one signal make the call. Reputation alone wouldn’t have caught this. Neither would link analysis, since the first hop is a Google URL and the final page doesn’t exist until a browser builds it. Instead, the detection approach weighs technical indicators alongside the apparent intent of the message, where its links actually end up, and the sending relationship behind it. Any one of those can be enough to act on. A detection built around a single signal inherits that signal’s blind spots, and this operator has put real effort into mapping them.

Where the analysis happens matters too. Gateways built to inspect mail in transit aren’t a great fit for calendar invites, and much of this campaign arrives as invites. Calendar invites need to be treated as a threat surface of their own, with the account’s full history used as context next to the technical signals.

Where the damage lands

A hijacked session leaves its trail in Google Workspace audit logs. A live session reaches mail, Drive, and the ability to grant OAuth access in the victim’s name, so the blast radius goes well past the inbox.

That raises a couple of hard questions for security teams. Who’s actually reviewing those audit logs, and how fast can they act on what they find? Could the team revoke sessions, contain OAuth grants, and reset the affected account within an hour? Plenty of programs can’t, and an attacker holding a live session can do a lot in an hour.

Operation CloudFire: going after the infrastructure

By late September, the researchers decided that tuning rules, retraining models, and updating agents wouldn’t solve this alone. Detection protects customers, but it does nothing about an operator who’s already prepping the next wave. So the team went after the infrastructure.

Analysts pulled the gateway and backend URLs as messages were being sent and reported them through Cloudflare’s abuse reporting system. Cloudflare’s abuse team confirmed the fake interstitial and the proxied Google sign-in page behind it, then put its own phishing warning in front of those destinations.

That had two effects. First, the attacker’s infrastructure got burned. Every reported gateway and endpoint had to be re-registered, re-pointed, and re-certified before the operator could send again. Second, it protected people well beyond any one company’s customers. Anyone who clicked a reported link saw a warning page instead of a credential form.

One month by the numbers

These figures only cover organizations that agreed to share data, so the real totals are higher. Over one month of Operation CloudFire, researchers recorded:

  • 68,676 campaign messages blocked
  • 2,112 unique malicious URLs analyzed
  • 897 unique domains taken down
  • 8,570 unique compromised sender addresses across 6,354 root domains

The messages also followed a clear rhythm, with sends tracking US business hours.

Message delivery by time of day

The sender count explains how the campaign earned trust. The attacker controlled each compromised account before the first invite went out, and each one sent invites to the account owner’s saved contacts, among others. Recipients saw a name or domain they knew, on a domain with a clean history, at a sensible time of day. Reputation feeds had no reason to flag any of it.

Where things stand now

The phishing themes have moved from calendar invites to Google Drive file and document share invites. Researchers haven’t seen a matching jump in other lures or tactics, and activity from this group seems to have scattered. For now, the campaign looks finished.

Messages detected by week
Domains registered by interval

That’s a snapshot, and it could change fast. Rebuilding the infrastructure is cheap, and the framework has been public since February. The operator also shipped an unfinished Microsoft 365 branch alongside the live Google code. It includes a stylesheet path, a second harness, and a title string that decodes to a Microsoft sign-in prompt. None of those paths resolve today, and adding the new brand would only mean dropping in a file, with no code changes. The follow-on is built and waiting.

The researchers see the theme rotation as ongoing iteration and expect the next pivot to look a lot like this one, just with a different brand on it.

The full technical breakdown, including indicators of compromise and a timeline, is in the companion whitepaper. Teams hunting for this activity in their own environments should start there.

item.title: New N-central Exploits Work Against Patched Servers, Enable Root RCE and Windows SYSTEM Access (2026)
item.description:
N-able on Thursday said it's investigating a new public disclosure containing claims of additional vulnerabilities in on-premise versions of N-central running version 2026.4.1 HF2.

"Based on our initial review, the server issue described depends on a non-default configuration in which the Legacy API is turned on and exposed to the public internet," N-able said in a new advisory. "Legacy API is turned off by default in the product and is not recommended."

The company is urging customers to disable Legacy API immediately, if not already. It also noted that hosted environments are not affected by this issue.

The incident impacts the following services -

  • N-central On-premise (Americas)
  • N-central On-premise (APAC)
  • N-central On-premise (Europe)

The development comes days after N-able released 2026.4.1.26 to address a number of security flaws disclosed by independent security researcher Sean Bales earlier this week. The vulnerabilities are collectively tracked under the name Able2Shell.

The new shortcoming, also revealed by Bales, have been codenamed 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell, adding the proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits successfully work against N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26), the update N-able released on November 10, 2026, to resolve Able2Shell.

According to the researcher, 4EverAble2Shell enables unauthenticated remote code execution with root privileges on N-central servers. Agent2Shell, on the other hand, leverages more than 10 zero-day vulnerabilities to run commands on managed Windows agents as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, assuming the attacker knows the target appliance ID.

Ryan Dewhurst, founder and CEO of Previdian, told The Hacker News that targeted N-central probing has been observed against 4EverAble2Shell within hours following the release of the PoC. The activity has originated from the IP address 157.20.241[.]16. There is no evidence of successful exploitation as of writing.

In the attack chain observed by the threat intelligence company, threat actors have been observed attempting to achieve initial code execution through a recently disclosed Apache Axis flaw (CVE-2026-90436, CVSS score: 9.8), followed by attempts to escalate privileges to root using 4EverAble2Shell, and then download and execute a shell script from 157.20.241[.]16 using curl.

item.title: Google Cloud Warns Three AMD Turin CPU Flaws Could Leak Data Across Processes in VMs (2026)
item.description:
Google Cloud VMs on AMD Turin chips need a guest OS patch and a stop-and-start to protect against three CPU side-channel flaws, Google said this week.

The company has already applied mitigations against attacks between VMs, and between VMs and the host. Inside a VM, the flaws may let an attacker with code on the same processor core infer data from other processes or the kernel.

The affected machine series are C4D, N4D, H4D, Z4D,, and G4, including bare-metal instances of C4D and Z4D. Turin is the code name for fifth-generation AMD EPYC processors.

All three flaws are Transient Scheduler Attacks (TSA). Two of them, TSA-SQ (CVE-2024-36350) and TSA-L1 (CVE-2024-36357), were first disclosed on July 8, 2025, for earlier EPYC processors.

AMD now says its Zen 5 processors, which include Turin, are "impacted differently from previously characterized AMD processors." The third flaw, CVE-2026-0004, is new. It may let an attacker who can run code on a system infer data in the processor's L1 data cache.

The Xen Project, which maintains the Xen hypervisor, calls the new flaw TSA-Fill. It also says an earlier statement has been corrected: "AMD had previously said that Zen5 CPUs were not vulnerable to TSA-SQ and TSA-L1."

Google rates the issue Medium. AMD classifies all three as local attacks with high attack complexity that require only low privileges, according to its Zen 5 bulletin and CVE-2026-0004 advisory.

As of today, none of the three is in the KEV catalog of exploited flaws kept by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Neither company reports any exploitation in its bulletins.

What Google Cloud Customers Need to Do

Google's security bulletin gives these steps for each service:

  • VMs: Install your OS vendor's fix when it ships. Starting this week, the company will update the CPU information that VMs report, so a patched guest kernel can turn on its mitigations. After that update reaches a VM, stop and start it. As the company puts it: "Rebooting the guest OS isn't enough."
  • Bare metal instances: If you run your own OS or hypervisor on a C4D or Z4D bare metal instance, apply your vendor's fixes when they are available.
  • Hypervisors inside a VM: The same CPU information update applies, so patched guest kernels can turn on their mitigations. Stop and start the VM once the update arrives.
  • GKE: Updated node images for Turin-based bare metal instances will be made available, and upgrading nodes picks up the CPU information update. As of today, the bulletin does not yet list them as available.
  • Cloud Run: No action is needed.

Customers on older Rome, Milan, and Genoa processors got the same stop-and-start instruction in an earlier bulletin at the time of the original disclosure on July 8, 2025.

The company lists nothing to do in the meantime for VMs whose OS vendor has not yet shipped a fix. It also does not say how to tell when the CPU information update has reached a VM.

A kernel commit that mitigates TSA on Zen 5, including the new variant, is in the Linux kernel source tree. As of today, Debian has fixed CVE-2026-0004 in its Linux kernel only in its unstable branch. Its security tracker still lists the kernels in bookworm, trixie, and forky as vulnerable.

For Turin servers on your own hardware, AMD says both platform firmware and OS updates are needed to mitigate the flaws fully. The mitigation may affect performance, and administrators should weigh the risk to their own workloads, according to its technical guidance.

The Xen Project has published hypervisor patches in its Xen advisory. It says microcode for all TSA flaws on Zen 5 has been in linux-firmware since September 23.

item.title: SCKit Malware Turns ScreenConnect Support Sessions Into Potential MSP Attack Paths (2026)
item.description:
The ongoing campaign targeting ConnectWise ScreenConnect deployments involves the exploitation of a now-patched critical security flaw in the remote access software, and not a new vulnerability, it has emerged.

Blackpoint Cyber's Adversary Pursuit Group (APG), which shared the details with The Hacker News, said the recovered attacker toolkit exploits CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS score: 9.9), an improper privilege management and missing authorization vulnerability that could allow an attacker to file transfer and execute through an active remote session without authorization or host confirmation.

The cybersecurity company confirmed that testing against a fully patched ScreenConnect client successfully prevents execution of the exploit's payload.

"Our testing confirmed that the exploit targets CVE-2026-84869 and that the existing patch successfully blocks it," APG researchers Sam Decker and Nevan Beal said. "That's an important finding for security teams."

"But the toolkit also includes capabilities to hijack authenticated operator sessions and use legitimate ScreenConnect management features to push malicious code. Patching addresses the known exploit, but it doesn't eliminate the risks associated with a compromised operator session."

Notably, the SCKit malware contains functionality called RelayTrap to reverse-pivot to infect the workstations of technicians who attempt to investigate suspicious activity in a managed endpoint. In other words, the activity abuses trusted functionality and does not rely on a software vulnerability once an attacker obtains a valid session.

The attack sequence makes use of the platform's built-in Run Command functionality to execute commands. This involves first checking for an existing ScreenConnect installation before downloading and running an attacker-controlled MSI installer ("sc.msi"), which then delivers the batch script dropper ("sckit-run.bat").

The batch script dropper subsequently contacts "ns.mo7sen[.]dev" to fetch a PowerShell decoder ("sckit-decoder.ps1") and ultimately deploy various components associated with the SCKit toolkit.

This includes a PowerShell script ("SilentForceInstall-WithUninstall.ps1") used to establish persistent remote access by deploying two unauthorized ScreenConnect Access clients, along with a set of scripts and C# code designed to interfere with existing ScreenConnect Guest sessions, including RelayTrap.

The component attempts a guest-to-host file execution technique associated with CVE-2026-84869 by replacing the legitimate ScreenConnect Guest and sending the SCKit payload back toward the connecting technician for execution.

If this action is successful, the malware tries to recover the technician's authenticated ScreenConnect browser sessions and leverage their existing management permissions to distribute commands across additional endpoints they have access to. As a result, an attacker can move beyond the original compromised system and into other customer environments through the same infrastructure used to administer them.

"Because these commands were executed through existing ScreenConnect agents, the attackers could deploy additional software under the NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM context without needing to establish a separate execution method on each machine," Blackpoint Cyber said.

"The unauthorized Access clients provide attackers with persistent control over the endpoint, while the RelayTrap components position the malware to intercept legitimate support connections. Rather than simply preventing administrators from accessing an infected machine, the toolkit attempts to use their next connection as an opportunity to extend the intrusion directly to the technician's workstation."

The end goal of the attack appears to target technicians, as they regularly connect to managed endpoints belonging to different customers, typically from workstations with access to administrative tools and authenticated management sessions. This enables the attackers to break out of the original endpoint and move the intrusion into an environment with potentially broader access and privileges.

Once the malware gets executed on the technician's machine, it shifts from remote support manipulation to session theft, searching the local browser data and process memory of the machine to recover an existing authenticated management session (i.e., .ASPXAUTH cookies) that can be used to propagate the malware to other endpoints without having to obtain their credentials.

"By first attempting to compromise a technician's workstation, then recover their authenticated ScreenConnect session, SCKit seeks to turn access to a single managed endpoint into an opportunity to reach other systems under that technician's control," the researchers said.

The Hacker News has contacted ConnectWise for comment, and we will update the story if we hear back.

It's worth noting that CVE-2026-84869 was previously exploited in a set of attacks in which threat actors leveraged ScreenConnect to distribute a malicious four-stage Visual Basic Script (VBScript) payload to newly connected systems and ultimately serve an XMRig cryptocurrency miner.

The vulnerability was added by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on September 11, 2026, requiring federal agencies to apply the fixes by September 14, 2026.

In response to the latest incident, ConnectWise has taken the precautionary step of disabling five third-party extensions in partner environments. However, Blackpoint Cyber said it found no technical link between those extensions and SCKit.

As of writing, there is no evidence that the activity has established successful propagation to a technician workstation or bypassed the vendor patch for CVE-2026-84869.

The findings reinforce the importance of patching ScreenConnect clients, and underscore the need for stronger operator-session protections, including tighter session validation and additional authentication for bulk administrative actions, Blackpoint Cyber noted.

"Organizations need to protect those sessions and put additional safeguards around high-impact administrative actions," the researchers said.

"For MSPs, the practical lesson is to investigate the management relationship, not only the endpoint. Rogue Access installations, administrative command history, technician workstations, and browser sessions all deserve attention, especially when support personnel have already connected to a suspected system."

RMM+ Authentication Flaw Found

Huntress, in an update, said it has identified a serious authentication flaw in versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 of RMM+, one of the five third-party ScreenConnect extensions that has already been blocked by ConnectWise.

"When an administrator had not configured an access key, the extension would accept a blank one, potentially allowing unauthorized commands to execute without going through ScreenConnect's normal authentication controls," the company said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.

RMM+ makes it possible for another tool to manage ScreenConnect sessions without a technician working through the console. It authenticates requests with a shared access key ("RMMPlus.AccessKey") stored in the extension's settings. However, in versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32, the key defaults to a blank value.

Because RMM+ operates independently of ScreenConnect's normal user accounts, roles, and authentication controls, an attacker could potentially execute commands on the device without bypassing multi-factor authentication.

"Commands reached endpoints across several ScreenConnect instances within minutes. There was no corresponding login activity and the commands appeared in the logs reviewed linked to RMM+."

It's worth mentioning here that while the toolkit possesses capabilities to exploit CVE-2026-84869, there is no evidence to suggest that an unpatched ScreenConnect client was the initial entry point for the attack.

"At this time, initial access appears to be linked to malicious ScreenConnect extensions, although we do not have sufficient evidence to confirm this," Beal, principal MDR analyst at Blackpoint, told The Hacker News.

"Identifying patient zero would require additional forensic evidence from affected environments. Similarly, while November 11 marks the earliest publicly reported activity, we cannot rule out earlier compromises without further investigation. Our findings confirm the toolkit's capabilities but do not establish when or how the initial compromise occurred."

When contacted for comment, a ConnectWise spokesperson told The Hacker news that it's aware of reports of malicious activity affecting a limited number of ScreenConnect partners and that it's actively investigating the incident.

"While the initial access method remains unconfirmed, our initial assessment suggests the activity may involve a threat actor's abuse of independent third-party extensions installed in partner environments," the spokesperson said.

"We have disabled the identified extensions where we can take action as a precaution and are advising on-premises partners to disable them immediately. The presence of these extensions alone does not establish compromise. We encourage partners to review the precautionary guidance in the ConnectWise Trust Center, where we will provide updates as information is validated."

(The story was updated after publication to include responses and insights from ConnectWise, Blackpoint Cyber, and Huntress.)

item.title: 186 Fake AI Domains Redirect Users to ClickFix Lures, Browser Malware, and Search Hijackers (2026)
item.description:
Cybersecurity researchers have found that lookalike domains masquerading as artificial intelligence (AI) tools are being used to serve ClickFix-style lures, browser-hijacking malware, and a set of extensions that hijack user searches.

This delivery pattern has been codenamed TypoPrompting by Island.

"AI-app lookalikes that turn an attempt to reach a familiar tool into a prompt to verify, install or run something else," the cybersecurity company said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

In all, the campaign spans 186 bogus domains spanning 27 AI brands, including Anthropic Claude, OpenAI ChatGPT, Google Gemini and Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM), Microsoft Copilot, SpaceXAI Grok, DeepSeek, Mistral, Perplexity, Midjourney, ElevenLabs, Lovable, and Cursor.

While one category leads to a ClickFix lure that serves a PowerShell command via a fake Cloudflare verification page, the second route takes unsuspecting users to "Security Check" pages that deliver a browser-hijacking malware called Net Guard. The third pathway sends users to a search-hijack extension family with 16 live Chrome Web Store listings and 972,000 declared users.

Some of the AI lookalike domains are listed below -

  • cloude[.]ai
  • cluade[.]ai
  • clsude[.]ai
  • chatlgpt[.]com
  • geimini[.]com
  • notebookklm[.]com
  • griok[.]com
  • preplexity[.]ai
  • deepceek[.]com
  • elevenlebs[.]io
  • copiot[.]com
  • midj0urney[.]org

An analysis of registration records shows that some of these domains, like cloude[.]ai and cluade[.]ai, were registered as early as July 13, 2023.

The use of parked domains for malware delivery is not new. In December 2025, Infoblox highlighted how domains without a current web page can be monetized to redirect visitors to sites that serve scams and malware after profiling the host and the device they are visiting from.

"When a domain owner opts into direct search, traffic to the domain is sold to advertisers who bid on keywords and traffic characteristics," the DNS threat intelligence firm noted at the time. "In practice, the site visitor is usually funneled through a series of traffic distribution systems (TDSs) operated by third-party advertising platforms, creating a complex web where a legitimate business model is weaponized for abuse."

In the case of the ClickFix route, the parked page initiates a redirect chain that fingerprints the web browser and collects the public IP address before displaying the fake Cloudflare verification page.

Island said the fingerprint gate script spans a broader set of 211 entry domains, including lookalikes of banks, insurers, and enterprise software, such as Scotiabank, Charles Schwab, Blue Cross Blue Shield, Verizon, ServiceNow, and Microsoft Azure.

These domains serve three types of lures -

  • Fake verification pages on Windows that are designed to run a clipboard command
  • Terminal or security updates on macOS that are designed to run a shell command
  • Archive download pages that instruct users to extract and run an executable

Separately, eight typosquat domains for Claude, DeepSeek, Copilot, ElevenLabs, and Voice AI lead to fake "Security Check" pages that ultimately deliver Net Guard.

While the app purports to be a Wi-Fi and DNS safety scanner and matches the MSIX hash for a legitimate app of the same name, it contains capabilities to run attacker-controlled JavaScript, change the default search engine while the user is idle, edit browser profiles, and install arbitrary Chrome extensions.

"The download from the 'Security Check' pages is the Microsoft Store app itself, unmodified," Oleg Zaytsev, Lead Security Researcher at Island, told The Hacker News. "It is byte-for-byte identical to Net Guard as Microsoft distributes it, and it carries Microsoft’s own Store signature."

"The hidden browser control comes with every copy, whether installed from the Store or from a typo site, and it switches itself on without asking. It waits until the user stops using the computer, then takes over Chrome's search settings and can run scripts inside the browser, following instructions from the operator's server."

The third route revolves around a lookalike domain for Perplexity ("preplexity[.]ai"), which redirects the browser to a browser extension called Quick Search that's available on the Chrome Web Store.

"The analyzed extension needs no executable JavaScript or declared permissions to perform its main action," Island said. "Its manifest overrides the default search provider with find.flashysearches[.]com . Searches made through that provider are sent to a third party. In a workplace, those queries can include internal hostnames, customer names and project details."

Quick Search is part of a larger set of 16 extensions, including GPT for Chrome, which has 80,000 users. In all, the extensions collectively have 972,000 users as of November 3, 2026.

"An address one letter away from an AI tool can lead to a very different request," Island said. "As these services become part of everyday work, reaching the right one should be a managed path, not a test of typing accuracy."

(The story was updated after publication to include a response from Island.)

Island said the fingerprint gate script spans a broader set of 211 entry domains, including lookalikes of banks, insurers, and enterprise software, such as Scotiabank, Charles Schwab, Blue Cross Blue Shield, Verizon, ServiceNow, and Microsoft Azure.

  • Terminal or security updates on macOS that are designed to run a shell command
  • Archive download pages that instruct users to extract and run an executable

While the app purports to be a Wi-Fi and DNS safety scanner and matches the MSIX hash for a legitimate app of the same name, it contains capabilities to run attacker-controlled JavaScript, change the default search engine while the user is idle, edit browser profiles, and install arbitrary Chrome extensions.

"The download from the 'Security Check' pages is the Microsoft Store app itself, unmodified," Oleg Zaytsev, Lead Security Researcher at Island, told The Hacker News. "It is byte-for-byte identical to Net Guard as Microsoft distributes it, and it carries Microsoft’s own Store signature."

"The hidden browser control comes with every copy, whether installed from the Store or from a typo site, and it switches itself on without asking. It waits until the user stops using the computer, then takes over Chrome's search settings and can run scripts inside the browser, following instructions from the operator's server."

The third route revolves around a lookalike domain for Perplexity ("preplexity[.]ai"), which redirects the browser to a browser extension called Quick Search that's available on the Chrome Web Store.

"The analyzed extension needs no executable JavaScript or declared permissions to perform its main action," Island said. "Its manifest overrides the default search provider with find.flashysearches[.]com . Searches made through that provider are sent to a third party. In a workplace, those queries can include internal hostnames, customer names and project details."

Quick Search is part of a larger set of 16 extensions, including GPT for Chrome, which has 80,000 users. In all, the extensions collectively have 972,000 users as of November 3, 2026.

"An address one letter away from an AI tool can lead to a very different request," Island said. "As these services become part of everyday work, reaching the right one should be a managed path, not a test of typing accuracy."

item.title: Citrix Patches 12 NetScaler and Secure Access Client Flaws, Including Authentication Bypass (2026)
item.description:

  • CVE-2026-107409 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory corruption vulnerability in DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (NetScaler configured with DNS Load Balancing over HTTPS)
  • CVE-2026-107410 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory overflow in NetScaler Push can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (NetScaler configured as Load Balancing virtual server  of type PUSH)
  • CVE-2026-107412 (CVSS score: 9.5) - Multiple memory overflow vulnerabilities can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior and DoS. (NetScaler configured as a Gateway or an AAA virtual server)
  • CVE-2026-107415 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory overflow vulnerability in Email OTP authentication can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (NetScaler ADC or NetScaler Gateway configured with an Email Action)
  • CVE-2026-111344 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory overflow vulnerability in Endpoint Analysis (EPA/EPAS) can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (NetScaler configured as a VPN virtual server or an authentication (AAA) virtual server with Endpoint Analysis)
  • CVE-2026-120864 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A memory overflow vulnerability in ICA proxy can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or DoS. (NetScaler configured as a Gateway VPN virtual server, an AAA virtual server, or a CR virtual server of type HDX)
